author: BrentDesk Research
headline: AVEVA chief executive joins Schneider Electric MEA summit line-up
deck: Schneider's proposition is that the equipment and the software controlling it should come from one supplier, and Gulf greenfield buyers are the best audience for it.
excerpt: AVEVA chief executive Caspar Herzberg appears alongside Schneider Electric's leadership at the MEA summit, representing an integrated hardware and software proposition.
content:
Among the executives Schneider Electric has confirmed for its Middle East and Africa Innovation Summit at ADNEC in Abu Dhabi on 15 and 16 September is Caspar Herzberg, chief executive of AVEVA. His presence alongside Schneider's own leadership — chief executive Olivier Blum, Manish Pant, Fredric Godemel, Pankaj Sharma, Hany Fouda, Walid Sheta and Amel Chadli — is the summit's commercial argument stated as a seating plan.

Schneider's position in industrial markets rests on selling the equipment and the software that runs it as one proposition. AVEVA supplies industrial software — engineering design, simulation, operations management, asset performance — and Schneider supplies the electrical distribution, control and automation hardware underneath. The pitch is that a customer buying both from one group gets an integrated system rather than an integration project.

The argument has a real technical basis. Industrial sites accumulate equipment and software from many vendors over decades, and the interfaces between them are where cost, delay and operational risk concentrate. A plant whose control system, electrical distribution, asset management software and engineering models share a data model genuinely does behave differently from one where each was procured separately and stitched together.

It is also much easier to sell to a customer building something new. An operator with an installed base of mixed vendors is being asked to replace working systems for an integration benefit that arrives only when the replacement is complete. A customer building a greenfield facility is choosing for the first time, and the integrated proposition costs nothing extra to adopt.

That is precisely why the Gulf is the right audience. The region is building industrial capacity, data centres, utilities and entire cities from nothing, at a rate few markets match. Every one of those is a greenfield decision, and this publication has covered the volume: the Saudi industrial cities programme, the data centre build-out including Alfanar's component manufacturing, the grid expansion connecting new generation, and the giga-project programmes represented at Saudi Mega Projects in Riyadh at the end of the month.

Schneider's own regional manufacturing commitment sits behind the pitch. The company has said it will take Saudi production from twelve lines to thirty-two by 2030 across plants in Riyadh and Dammam totalling more than 35,000 square metres, with a facility at King Salman Energy Park building distributed control, emergency shutdown and compressor control systems.

The summit is themed around advancing energy technology to power intelligence and resilience, with Forbes Middle East, Bain & Company and Deloitte as partners. No session-level agenda or product launches had been published in advance.
